stories.bridge: Enigma is why cryptography matters and why it must be done right. Now let's learn the real thing — from classical ciphers to the mathematics that replaced them.

figures.name: Alan Turing
figures.role: Designed the Bombe at Bletchley Park

figures.name: Tommy Flowers
figures.role: Built Colossus, the first programmable electronic computer (1943)

stories.hook: In December 1932, a 27-year-old Pole broke the 'unbreakable' cipher — seven years before the war began.
stories.narrative: Marian Rejewski worked for the Polish Biuro Szyfrów, the cipher bureau, which had the foresight to hire mathematicians instead of linguists. Using group theory — pure mathematics — and a spy's gift of Enigma documents, Rejewski broke the German Enigma cipher in December 1932 and built the 'bomba,' a machine to find the daily key. When Poland fell in 1939, the Poles handed everything to Britain and France — one of the most consequential intelligence gifts in history. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing — 27, already famous for his 1936 paper on computability — took Rejewski's bomba and redesigned it into the Bombe, which attacked the naval Enigma's far harder settings; the first went operational in March 1940. Meanwhile the Germans' other cipher, the Lorenz teleprinter used by high command, was broken mathematically before anyone had even seen the machine — and to exploit it, Tommy Flowers, a Post Office engineer, built Colossus: the world's first programmable electronic digital computer, operational in December 1943, using 1,500 vacuum tubes to chew through Lorenz traffic. The secret was kept for thirty years — the Colossus engineers were told to destroy the machines and never speak. When the story finally emerged in the 1970s, it rewrote computing history: the computer was born, in part, as a codebreaking machine. For your certificate, Enigma is the founding parable: cryptography decides wars, mathematics beats machinery, and operational security — the Germans' sloppy procedures doomed Enigma as much as the math — is half the battle. Learn the ciphers, but learn the procedures harder. The secrecy lasted thirty years — Colossus's engineers were ordered to destroy the machines and stay silent, so the computer's birth certificate was sealed until the 1970s. When it emerged, computing history had to be rewritten: the programmable electronic computer was, in part, a codebreaking machine. Your certificate's cryptography module starts here because everything since — from DES to AES — is the same story with new math.
stories.title: The story behind Enigma
verifiedClaims: Rejewski broke Enigma in December 1932 for the Polish cipher bureau
Turing's Bombe became operational in March 1940 at Bletchley Park
Flowers's Colossus was operational in December 1943

stories.bridge: AES won because it was open, elegant, and fast. Now let's learn the symmetric cryptography you'll actually deploy — and why the standard matters.
stories.hook: In 1997, the US government held an open contest to replace its cipher — and two Belgians won.
stories.narrative: The Data Encryption Standard, adopted in 1977, was dying of old age: its 56-bit key, adequate in the seventies, had become brute-forceable — proven in 1998 when the EFF's 'Deep Crack' machine broke a DES key in 56 hours for $250,000. NIST's response was radical for a government: an open, public competition. In 1997 it called for candidates; fifteen ciphers were submitted from around the world, five made the finals, and cryptographers spent two years attacking them all in public. On October 2, 2000, NIST selected Rijndael — designed by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen, two Belgian cryptographers — for its combination of security, performance, and elegance: a clean substitution-permutation network that ran fast in both software and hardware. It became FIPS-197, the Advanced Encryption Standard, in November 2001. The contest model was the real innovation: Kerckhoffs's principle industrialized, the cipher trusted because it survived the world's best attacks in the open. AES now encrypts everything — your disk, your messages, the government's top secrets (it's approved for classified data). No practical attack has dented it in over two decades. For your certificate, AES is the standard you'll implement and the story you'll tell: when someone asks why you trust it, the answer is 1997–2001 — the open contest, the public cryptanalysis, the Belgian elegance. Security through transparency, not obscurity. The Belgian winners were the underdogs: Rijndael beat better-funded finalists on elegance and speed, and Daemen and Rijmen gave the design away freely. The contest's openness was the point — NIST wanted a cipher the world could trust because the world had attacked it. Two decades without a practical break is the verdict. In this module you'll implement AES modes and learn why the contest model, not the cipher alone, is what you're actually trusting. Trust the contest, not the cipher alone.
stories.title: The story behind AES
verifiedClaims: NIST's AES competition ran 1997–2000; Rijndael was selected October 2, 2000
The EFF's Deep Crack broke DES in 1998

stories.bridge: Stuxnet proved the air gap is a story we tell, not a control we have. Now let's learn OT and IoT risk — where the consequences are physical.
stories.hook: In June 2010, a small antivirus firm in Belarus found a worm too sophisticated to be criminal.
stories.narrative: VirusBlokAda's Sergey Ulasen was investigating customer machines when he found something unprecedented: a worm of extraordinary complexity — four zero-day exploits, stolen digital certificates from real companies, and a payload that did nothing to normal computers. Researchers worldwide converged on it, and the picture that emerged was stunning: Stuxnet was a cyberweapon aimed at Iran's Natanz uranium enrichment plant. Once inside, it hunted for Siemens PLCs driving the centrifuges, then subtly varied their speeds — destroying the equipment while reporting normal readings to the operators. It was the first malware designed to cause physical destruction, crossing the line from espionage to sabotage. The sophistication pointed to nation-states — widely attributed to a US-Israeli operation — and the implications rewrote industrial security: the plant was air-gapped, yet the worm arrived (likely via USB), proving that isolation is a delay, not a defense. For OT and IoT risk, Stuxnet is the founding case study and the permanent warning: operational technology runs the physical world — power, water, manufacturing, pipelines — on systems designed before security existed, with protocols that trust everything and lifespans measured in decades. The module you're entering teaches you to assess that risk honestly: inventory the unpatchable, segment the unsegmentable, and monitor the protocols that were never meant to be attacked. Stuxnet was 2010. The PLCs are still out there. The attribution — widely reported as a US-Israeli operation — was never officially confirmed, which is itself the lesson: cyberweapons live in the gray zone between espionage and war, with no declared rules. The Natanz centrifuges were the target; the precedent was the payload. In this module you'll learn OT risk assessment for the world Stuxnet revealed: air gaps as delay, PLCs as targets, physical consequences as the stakes. Air gaps delay; they don't defend. Plan accordingly.  Assess every OT environment as if Stuxnet already visited.
stories.title: The story behind Stuxnet
verifiedClaims: Stuxnet was discovered in June 2010 by Belarus's VirusBlokAda
It targeted Siemens PLCs at Iran's Natanz facility using four zero-days
It was the first malware designed for physical destruction

stories.bridge: The Clipper fight set the terms of every privacy debate since. Now let's learn policy, privacy, and governance — where the technology meets the law.

figures.name: Matt Blaze
figures.role: AT&T researcher; broke the Clipper key-escrow protocol (1994)

stories.hook: On April 16, 1993, the White House announced a chip that would keep America safe — by keeping a copy of everyone's key.
stories.narrative: The Clipper chip was the Clinton administration's answer to strong encryption: a government-designed chip, using the classified Skipjack cipher, for secure phones — with a catch. Each chip had a unique key, split and held in escrow by two government agencies, so law enforcement could decrypt with a court order. The pitch was 'security with accountability'; the industry heard 'a backdoor by design.' The crypto community revolted — the cypherpunks, the EFF, working cryptographers — arguing that key escrow created a single point of failure and a precedent for government-mandated weakness. Then in 1994, Matt Blaze, a researcher at AT&T Bell Labs, published the technical kill shot: 'Protocol Failure in the Escrowed Encryption Standard' showed the escrow mechanism itself could be defeated — an attacker could use the chip while evading the escrow field, getting the security without the surveillance. The mathematics didn't care about the policy. Clipper died commercially — almost nobody bought the phones — and the episode became the first crypto war's defining battle, establishing the industry's position: you cannot build a backdoor only the good guys can use. The debate never ended — it resurfaced over the FBI and Apple in 2016, over messaging encryption ever since. For your certificate's governance module, Clipper is the essential history: policy and technology are not separate subjects. Every regulation you'll study, from data-breach notification to privacy law, is downstream of fights like this one. Learn the technology cold, because the policy arguments are won by people who understand what the math allows. The crypto wars' first battle set the industry's permanent position: exceptional access breaks the mathematics for everyone, because a backdoor is just a vulnerability with a badge. The fight recurs — Apple vs. FBI in 2016, messaging encryption today — with the same 1993 arguments. In your governance module, Clipper is the precedent: policy must respect what the math allows, or the math routes around the policy.
stories.title: The story behind the Clipper chip
verifiedClaims: The White House announced the Clipper chip April 16, 1993, with key escrow
Blaze's 1994 paper broke the escrow protocol
The chip failed commercially; the episode defined the crypto wars
